doc.title: Al Chez interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, February 13, 2019

chapter: Getting and negotiating the Letterman job
title: Sweeps hire and getting the Letterman job on air
summary: After touring with Tower of Power and the Robert Cray Band, Chez was hired for sweeps and Letterman said on air that the kid stays; the 17 years gave him a pension.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: So then when they moved to CBS I was out on the West Coast playing with Tower of Power and the Robert Cray Band. And I did that for a while. I came back home and I called Shaffer up and I said, “I really don’t want to go on the road anymore,” You know Tom Malone was playing trumpet and trombone. Great trombone player. Trumpet owner. So I was like if you want to add a trumpet full time I won’t go on the road anymore. Took a shot. Called him up. So time went by and I didn’t hear anything, so I get a call from the Letterman Show saying that they’re doing the sweeps period. The sweeps period are what ratings are based upon. And there’s three of them a year, and depending on how many Nielsen families watch that’s how much a minute of commercial time is worth. Okay? That’s how you get the ratings. That’s how they pay for commercial time. So they always put the best guests on during sweeps. They want to bolster the band. They get the most musical you know, the best musical guests on. So they hired me to do the three weeks of sweeps period, as an extra trumpet player onto the band. So I get hired and I do the three weeks, and it was the last day of sweeps and on the air David Letterman looks over and he goes, “Paul, the new trumpet player you know, sounds great” and then he looks at me. And “Paul Shaffer goes, ‘Well that’s Al Chez’” ba-ba-ba-ba. And Letterman looks at me and he goes, “Well did you get the gig or what, kid?” And I’m like, “I don’t know.” You know? And Paul goes, “Well we’re waiting to hear from you, Dave.” And on the air Letterman goes, “Well as far as I’m concerned the kid stays.” So the next day the CBS attorney is calling my house and he wants to negotiate a three year contract on CBS to be the trumpet player on the show. And he wants the number of my lawyer. So I’m like yeah okay. So I’m like, “Let me just call you back.” And I’m looking in the phone book, because I’m like this Jersey rat who’s been on the road, I don’t have a lawyer. Then I called: “Hey who’s your lawyer?” I didn’t have a lawyer. You know what I mean? But I had to join the union going back to your thing, to be on the show. And the union’s been great. Seventeen years on network television, you get a pension now, which is a beautiful thing. A musician with a pension. There is such a thing.
Right here. I haven’t collected it yet but it’s there.
